--- course-unit: ch09-bayesian-inference status: complete --- # Bayesian inference ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own. ::: ## Learning goals Chapter 8 treated the parameters as fixed unknowns and summarised uncertainty through the sampling distribution of an estimator. The Bayesian approach instead treats the parameters as random variables and updates a **prior** belief into a **posterior** using the data [@gelman2013]. This chapter fits the same SIR model to the same kind of simulated case reports, but with [Turing.jl](https://turinglang.org/). By the end you should be able to - state Bayes' theorem for the SIR observation model and identify the prior, likelihood, and posterior; - write a probabilistic model with the `@model` macro and sample it with the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS); - assess convergence with $\hat R$ and effective sample size using [MCMCChains.jl](https://turinglang.org/MCMCChains.jl/stable/); and - summarise parameter uncertainty and propagate it into a **posterior predictive** check. ## Model assumptions and classification The process and observation models are unchanged from the previous two chapters: a deterministic SIR ODE with cumulative incidence @eq-sir-cumulative and a Poisson observation model @eq-poisson with full reporting. As in Chapter 8 we infer $\theta = (i_0, \beta)$ with $c=10$ and $\gamma=0.25$ fixed. The difference is entirely in the treatment of uncertainty. | Aspect | Frequentist (Ch. 8) | Bayesian (this chapter) | | --- | --- | --- | | Parameters | fixed unknowns | random variables with a prior | | Output | point estimate + confidence interval | posterior distribution | | Uncertainty | sampling variability of the estimator | posterior probability | | Engine | optimisation (`Optimization.jl`) | MCMC sampling (`Turing.jl`) | ## Equations Bayes' theorem combines the prior density $p(\theta)$ with the likelihood $p(y_{1:n}\mid\theta)$ — the same Poisson likelihood whose logarithm is @eq-loglik — to give the posterior $$ p(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) = \frac{p(y_{1:n}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)}{p(y_{1:n})}, \qquad p(y_{1:n}) = \int p(y_{1:n}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta . $$ {#eq-bayes} The normalising constant $p(y_{1:n})$ is intractable here, so we never compute it directly; instead NUTS draws samples $\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(m)}$ whose histogram approximates the posterior. We place weakly informative Beta priors that respect the natural $[0,1]$ range of both parameters, $$ i_0 \sim \operatorname{Beta}(1, 20), \qquad \beta \sim \operatorname{Beta}(1, 10), $$ {#eq-priors} with prior means $1/21 \approx 0.048$ and $1/11 \approx 0.091$: broad enough to be uninformative near the truth ($i_0=0.01$, $\beta=0.05$) but supported only on plausible values. Any posterior expectation, such as the predictive incidence, is an integral against the posterior that we estimate by averaging over the draws. ## Julia implementation ::: {#setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using OrdinaryDiffEq using SciMLSensitivity using Turing using MCMCChains using Distributions using StableRNGs using CairoMakie CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png") colors = (data = :grey20, post = :steelblue, band = (:steelblue, 0.3), truth = :firebrick) ``` ::: ### Process kernel and simulated data We reuse the deterministic kernel and the Poisson observation model to generate a reproducible dataset, exactly as in Chapter 8. ::: {#cell-data .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t) S, I, R, C = u β, c, γ = p N = S + I + R infection = β * c * I / N * S recovery = γ * I @inbounds begin du[1] = -infection du[2] = infection - recovery du[3] = recovery du[4] = infection end return nothing end tmax = 40.0 tspan = (0.0, tmax) obstimes = 1.0:1.0:tmax u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0] p = [0.05, 10.0, 0.25] prob_ode = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p) sol = solve(prob_ode, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0) incidence = Array(sol)[4, 2:end] .- Array(sol)[4, 1:(end - 1)] data = rand.(StableRNG(20240607), Poisson.(incidence)) ``` ::: {#data .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 40-element Vector{Int64}: 2 8 4 10 10 12 14 21 42 36 ⋮ 6 3 4 5 5 3 3 1 4 ``` ::: ::: ### The probabilistic model The `@model` macro turns @eq-bayes and @eq-priors into executable code. The `~` statements declare the priors; the loop declares the Poisson likelihood of each observation given the model incidence. We reject failed ODE solves and floor the Poisson rate by a negligible constant so that the sampler never evaluates `Poisson(0)` on the burned-out tail of the epidemic. ::: {#cell-turing-model .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @model function bayes_sir(y, prob) l = length(y) i₀ ~ Beta(1.0, 20.0) β ~ Beta(1.0, 10.0) I = i₀ * 1000.0 u0 = [1000.0 - I, I, 0.0, 0.0] θ = [β, 10.0, 0.25] prob = remake(prob; u0 = u0, p = θ, tspan = (0.0, float(l))) sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0) if !SciMLBase.successful_retcode(sol) Turing.@addlogprob! -Inf return nothing end C = Array(sol)[4, :] X = C[2:end] .- C[1:(end - 1)] for i in 1:l y[i] ~ Poisson(max(X[i], 0.0) + 1e-6) end return nothing end ``` ::: {#turing-model .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` bayes_sir (generic function with 2 methods) ``` ::: ::: ### Sampling with NUTS We draw three independent chains of 500 iterations each. Multiple chains are what make the $\hat R$ diagnostic meaningful, and NUTS uses automatic differentiation through the ODE solver, enabled here by [SciMLSensitivity.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/). The `StableRNG` seed makes the run reproducible. The sample counts here are modest so that the chapter runs in seconds; a real analysis wants more, and $\hat{R}$ with the effective sample size are what tell you when you have enough. ::: {#cell-sample .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} model = bayes_sir(data, prob_ode) chain = sample(StableRNG(2), model, NUTS(0.8), MCMCSerial(), 500, 3; chain_type = MCMCChains.Chains, progress = false) summarize(chain) ``` ::: {#sample .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
  parameters      mean       std      mcse   ess_bulk   ess_tail      rhat   e ⋯
      Symbol   Float64   Float64   Float64    Float64    Float64   Float64     ⋯

          i₀    0.0091    0.0011    0.0001   438.6383   526.6950    1.0119     ⋯
           β    0.0500    0.0010    0.0000   458.1696   478.6566    1.0070     ⋯

                                                                1 column omitted
``` ::: ::: ::: ## Validation MCMC results are only trustworthy once the chains have converged. The potential scale reduction factor $\hat R$ should be close to $1$ (values above $\approx 1.01$ suggest the chains disagree), and the effective sample size (ESS) should be comfortably large. We also confirm that the posterior concentrates near the true parameters. ::: {#cell-diagnostics .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} truth = (i₀ = 0.01, β = 0.05) i0_mat = Array(chain[:, :i₀, :]) β_mat = Array(chain[:, :β, :]) i0s = vec(i0_mat) βs = vec(β_mat) (max_rhat = maximum(rhat(chain).nt.rhat), min_ess = minimum(ess(chain).nt.ess), posterior_mean = (i₀ = round(mean(i0s); digits = 4), β = round(mean(βs); digits = 4)), truth = truth) ``` ::: {#diagnostics .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (max_rhat = 1.0119284999004239, min_ess = 438.6383389673823, posterior_mean = (i₀ = 0.0091, β = 0.05), truth = (i₀ = 0.01, β = 0.05)) ``` ::: ::: The trace plots should look like well-mixed "fuzzy caterpillars" that overlap across chains, and the marginal densities should be unimodal and bracket the true values. ::: {#cell-fig-diagnostics .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (900, 560)) for (row, (name, mat, tru)) in enumerate((("i₀", i0_mat, truth.i₀), ("β", β_mat, truth.β))) axt = Axis(fig[row, 1]; xlabel = "Iteration", ylabel = name) for ch in 1:size(mat, 2) lines!(axt, 1:size(mat, 1), mat[:, ch]) end axd = Axis(fig[row, 2]; xlabel = name, ylabel = "Density") density!(axd, vec(mat); color = (colors.post, 0.4), strokecolor = colors.post, strokewidth = 2) vlines!(axd, [tru]; color = colors.truth, linewidth = 2) end fig ``` ::: {#fig-diagnostics .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Trace plots (left) and marginal posterior densities (right) for i₀ and β. The three chains overlap, and the densities (blue) concentrate around the true values (red). ::: ::: ### Posterior predictive check A posterior that fits well should reproduce the data when pushed back through the model. We draw parameter pairs from the posterior, simulate incidence for each, and summarise the resulting curves by pointwise $95\%$ intervals — a Monte Carlo estimate of the posterior predictive integral implied by @eq-bayes. ::: {#cell-fig-posterior-predictive .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function incidence_at(i₀, β, l) I = i₀ * 1000.0 prob_pp = remake(prob_ode; u0 = [1000.0 - I, I, 0.0, 0.0], p = [β, 10.0, 0.25], tspan = (0.0, float(l))) solp = solve(prob_pp, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0) C = Array(solp)[4, :] return C[2:end] .- C[1:(end - 1)] end l = length(data) idx = rand(StableRNG(3), 1:length(βs), 200) curves = reduce(hcat, [incidence_at(i0s[k], βs[k], l) for k in idx]) lower = [quantile(curves[t, :], 0.025) for t in 1:l] upper = [quantile(curves[t, :], 0.975) for t in 1:l] median_curve = [quantile(curves[t, :], 0.5) for t in 1:l] fig = Figure(size = (760, 420)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Time (days)", ylabel = "New cases per day") band!(ax, collect(obstimes), lower, upper; color = colors.band, label = "95% band") lines!(ax, collect(obstimes), median_curve; color = colors.post, linewidth = 3, label = "Posterior median") scatter!(ax, collect(obstimes), data; color = colors.data, label = "Data") axislegend(ax; position = :rt) fig ``` ::: {#fig-posterior-predictive .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Posterior predictive interval for daily incidence (95% band and median, blue) against the observed case reports (grey). The band tracks the data across the whole epidemic. ::: ::: ## Interpretation and limitations The posterior concentrates near the true parameters, the chains converge ($\hat R \approx 1$), and the predictive band envelops the data — a coherent story that also carries caveats. The priors of @eq-priors are a modelling choice: overly tight priors can dominate a small dataset, while flat priors on positive parameters can let the sampler wander into regions where the ODE misbehaves, which is why we guarded the solve and floored the rate. NUTS is far more efficient than random-walk MCMC, but each leapfrog step re-solves the ODE and differentiates through it, so the method is more expensive than the optimisation of Chapter 8 — the small sample counts here favour speed over the precision a production analysis would demand. The non-identifiability of $\beta$ and $c$ noted previously persists: the posterior for $\beta$ is conditional on the assumed contact rate. Finally, the Poisson likelihood still assumes equidispersion; a negative-binomial likelihood @eq-negbin would add a dispersion parameter and typically widen the posterior. Bayesian inference makes all of these assumptions explicit and propagates their consequences directly into the predictive distribution, which is its central practical advantage. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch09-ex1} Replace the Beta priors in @eq-priors with uniform priors $i_0 \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0, 1)$ and $\beta \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0, 1)$ and re-run the sampler. Compare the posterior means, the $\hat R$ values, and the width of the $95\%$ posterior predictive band with the Beta-prior results. Discuss whether the data are informative enough that the choice of prior barely matters here. ### Exercise 2 {#ch09-ex2} Add the recovery rate $\gamma$ as a third estimated parameter with prior $\gamma \sim \operatorname{Beta}(2, 8)$, updating the model accordingly. Report the posterior summaries and the pairwise posterior correlation between $\beta$ and $\gamma$ (for example from `Array(chain[:, :β, :])` and the corresponding $\gamma$ draws). Relate any strong correlation you find to the identifiability discussion in this chapter and in Chapter 8. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/09-bayesian-inference.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/09-bayesian-inference.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/09-bayesian-inference.jl)
